expectedText:
WHEN THE CLOCK STARTS ON A FEHA OR WRONGFUL-TERMINATION CLAIM: ACCRUAL AT ACTUAL TERMINATION AND THE CONTINUING VIOLATION DOCTRINE (GOV. CODE §§ 12960, 12993; ROMANO V. ROCKWELL INTERNAT.; RICHARDS V. CH2M HILL; YANOWITZ V. L’OREAL USA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California law on when the filing clock starts on a Fair Employment and Housing Act claim and on a wrongful-termination claim, and on the continuing violation doctrine, which is the rule that governs whether conduct occurring before that clock started can still be part of the claim. It is prepared in connection with the separation of Jordan Lee from Acme, Inc., where the position held was Project Engineer, the date the employer first communicated that the employment would end is stated as March 2, 2026, the date the employment actually ended is stated as August 28, 2026, and the earliest workplace conduct the employee describes is stated as beginning November 14, 2022. Those dates are as supplied by the person preparing this sheet; nothing here verifies them. This sheet is a description of published statutes and California Supreme Court decisions. It is not a complaint, not a filing with the Civil Rights Department, not a court document, not a calculation of any deadline in any particular matter, and not a determination that any conduct described by anyone was unlawful, that any claim exists, or that any claim is timely or untimely.

THE FEHA ADMINISTRATIVE FILING DEADLINE THE DOCTRINE OPERATES AGAINST
The continuing violation doctrine is a rule about a filing deadline, so it only makes sense against that deadline. Government Code section 12960 governs the procedure for complaints of practices made unlawful by the FEHA’s employment provisions. Subdivision (c) allows any person claiming to be aggrieved by an alleged unlawful practice to file a verified written complaint with the Civil Rights Department. Subdivision (e)(5) sets the period for an employment complaint under Article 1 of Chapter 6 (Government Code section 12940 and following) at three years from the date the unlawful practice or refusal to cooperate occurred, and subdivision (b) provides that filing an intake form counts as filing, with the verified complaint relating back to the intake form. The statutory period was one year when the decisions described in the rest of this sheet were written; Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. quoted the one-year version of section 12960 as it then read. Section 12993, subdivision (a) supplies the interpretive instruction the courts applied to that period: the FEHA is to be construed liberally. Whether any complaint concerning Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. was filed, and when, is not addressed here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Any person claiming to be aggrieved by an alleged unlawful practice may file with the department a verified complaint, in writing, that shall state the name and address of the person, employer, labor organization, or employment agency alleged to have committed the unlawful practice complained of, and that shall set forth the particulars thereof and contain other information as may be required by the department."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12960(c) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Gov't Code § 12960(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12960.)
  "A complaint alleging a violation of Section 51.9 of the Civil Code or any other violation of Article 1 (commencing with Section 12940) of Chapter 6 shall not be filed after the expiration of three years from the date upon which the unlawful practice or refusal to cooperate occurred."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12960(e)(5) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Gov't Code § 12960(e)(5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12960.)
  "For purposes of this section, filing a complaint means filing an intake form with the department and the operative date of the verified complaint relates back to the filing of the intake form."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12960(b) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Gov't Code § 12960(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12960.)
  "The provisions of this part shall be construed liberally for the accomplishment of the purposes of this part."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12993(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Gov't Code § 12993(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12993.)
  "No complaint may be filed after the expiration of one year from the date upon which the alleged unlawful practice or refusal to cooperate occurred"
  — Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. (2001) 26 Cal.4th 798, 26 Cal.4th 798, 811 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2633435/richards-v-ch2m-hill-inc/)
  Known gap: The three-year period in section 12960, subdivision (e)(5) reflects the version of the section most recently amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 321 (S.B. 477), effective January 1, 2026; the extension of the period from one year to three was made by Stats. 2019, Ch. 709 (A.B. 9), which this sheet did not separately fetch and which stated that it did not revive lapsed claims. This clause does not quote the several other filing periods in subdivision (e) (Civil Code sections 51, 51.5, 51.7, 52.5, 54, 54.1, 54.2; Government Code section 11135 and following; Labor Code section 1197.5), the subdivision (e)(6) extensions, the subdivision (f) tolling rule for the time to file a civil action, or the separate deadline in Government Code section 12965 for filing a civil action after a right-to-sue notice, all of which are addressed by this corpus’s separate FEHA administrative complaint sheet. The quoted sentence from Richards reproduces section 12960 as it read in 2001 and is not current law. No assertion is made here about which period applies to any conduct involving Jordan Lee.

A DISCHARGE CLAIM ACCRUES AT THE ACTUAL TERMINATION, NOT AT THE NOTICE OF IT
Romano v. Rockwell Internat., Inc. answered when the clock starts when an employee is told in advance that the employment will end. The employee there was notified in December 1988 that his employment would end, and it ended on May 31, 1991 — an interval of two and a half years during which he continued to be paid. The employer argued, relying on federal authority, that the period ran from the unequivocal notice. The California Supreme Court held otherwise for the FEHA claim, reasoning from the statutory word “occurred”: because section 12960 runs from the date the unlawful practice occurred, and because a discharge is the termination of employment, the practice has not occurred on the date notice is given. The Court added practical reasons — the date of actual termination is usually undisputed while notice is often oral, conditional, or equivocal, and a notice-based rule would force employees to file while still employed, over a harm that had not happened yet. In the separation of Jordan Lee from Acme, Inc., the notice date and the termination date are stated as March 2, 2026 and August 28, 2026; which legal consequence follows from those particular dates is not determined here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "In this case we consider when the statute of limitations begins to run in a wrongful termination case in which the plaintiff has alleged causes of action sounding in contract and tort, as well as violations of the California Fair Employment and Housing Act."
  — Romano v. Rockwell Internat., Inc. (1996) 14 Cal.4th 479, 14 Cal.4th 479, 483-484 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607863/romano-v-rockwell-international-inc/)
  "If the administrative complaint must be filed within one year “after” the unlawful practice—here, a discharge—“occurred,” then for the purpose of that complaint, the administrative cause of action must accrue and the statute of limitations must run from the time of actual termination. It would not run from the earlier date of notification of discharge, because on that date the unlawful practice (that is, the discharge) had not yet “occurred.”"
  — Romano v. Rockwell Internat., Inc. (1996) 14 Cal.4th 479, 14 Cal.4th 479, 493 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607863/romano-v-rockwell-international-inc/)
  "Unlike notice of termination, which frequently is oral and may be conditional or equivocal, the date of actual termination is a date that in most cases is subject to little dispute."
  — Romano v. Rockwell Internat., Inc. (1996) 14 Cal.4th 479, 14 Cal.4th 479, 494 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607863/romano-v-rockwell-international-inc/)
  "We conclude, therefore, that the date that triggers the running of the limitations period under the FEHA is the date of actual termination."
  — Romano v. Rockwell Internat., Inc. (1996) 14 Cal.4th 479, 14 Cal.4th 479, 495 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607863/romano-v-rockwell-international-inc/)
  Known gap: Romano was decided in 1996, when the section 12960 period was one year; the reasoning is about which date the period runs from, not about how long the period is. The opinion also disapproved a contrary Court of Appeal decision, Regents of the University of California v. Superior Court (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 1710, and discussed Delaware State College v. Ricks (1980) 449 U.S. 250 and Chardon v. Fernandez (1981) 454 U.S. 6, along with out-of-state authority; none of those decisions was independently fetched for this sheet and each is reported only as Romano describes it. Romano concerned an actual discharge on a fixed future date; it did not decide when a claim accrues where the employee resigns, and the Court noted that the concern about an employee controlling the accrual date “is not implicated in the case of an actual discharge.” Whether the communication recorded as March 2, 2026 was a notice of termination at all is not determined here.

THE SAME ACCRUAL DATE FOR THE CONTRACT CLAIM AND THE PUBLIC-POLICY TORT CLAIM
Romano applied the same accrual date to the employee’s other theories. On the contract side, where the alleged promise was not to terminate without good cause, the Court held the breach occurred at termination; alternatively, treating the advance notice as an anticipatory repudiation, an injured party may disregard the repudiation and wait for the time of performance, so the period did not begin until actual termination. On the tort side, the Court explained that because the wrongful-discharge tort recognized in Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. is defined as a limit imposed by law on the employer’s power of dismissal, it is the dismissal that breaches the duty, and the cause of action accrues then. The practical point the Court drew from its own facts was that there is little reason to require a claim while the termination decision may still be reversed and compensation may never be interrupted. Whether Jordan Lee has any contract or public-policy claim against Acme, Inc. is not addressed here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "With respect to Romano’s claim that the termination of his employment constituted a breach of an alleged implied contract not to terminate employment without good cause, and of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, it appears that the breach of this implied contract and covenant occurred at the time of termination."
  — Romano v. Rockwell Internat., Inc. (1996) 14 Cal.4th 479, 14 Cal.4th 479, 490 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607863/romano-v-rockwell-international-inc/)
  "Accordingly, we conclude that the statute of limitations applicable to the contract claims began to run at the time Romano’s employment actually was terminated, and that the causes of action for breach of contract were timely filed."
  — Romano v. Rockwell Internat., Inc. (1996) 14 Cal.4th 479, 14 Cal.4th 479, 491 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607863/romano-v-rockwell-international-inc/)
  "Accordingly, when an employee alleges that his or her employment has been terminated in violation of public policy, a cause of action will accrue at the time of dismissal for the purpose of the statute of limitations."
  — Romano v. Rockwell Internat., Inc. (1996) 14 Cal.4th 479, 14 Cal.4th 479, 501 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607863/romano-v-rockwell-international-inc/)
  "As we observed in connection with the FEHA claims discussed above, there is little reason to require the employee to bring a claim when the termination decision still may be reversed and compensation may never be interrupted."
  — Romano v. Rockwell Internat., Inc. (1996) 14 Cal.4th 479, 14 Cal.4th 479, 502 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607863/romano-v-rockwell-international-inc/)
  "Because a cause of action for wrongful discharge in violation of public policy accrues at the time of termination of employment, we conclude that the statute of limitations applicable to such a cause of action begins to run at the time of actual termination."
  — Romano v. Rockwell Internat., Inc. (1996) 14 Cal.4th 479, 14 Cal.4th 479, 503 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607863/romano-v-rockwell-international-inc/)
  Known gap: Which limitations period applies to a given claim is a separate question from when that period starts, and this clause addresses only the second. In Romano the parties did not dispute which periods applied — the employer asserted the one-year period of Code of Civil Procedure section 340 for the public-policy tort, the one-year period of Government Code section 12960 for the FEHA claims, and the two-year period of Code of Civil Procedure section 339 for the contract claims — so the case turned only on accrual. Those sections are not quoted here, and the general two-year personal-injury period now in Code of Civil Procedure section 335.1 was added by Stats. 2002, Ch. 448, effective January 1, 2003, after Romano was decided. The anticipatory-repudiation discussion rests on Taylor v. Johnston (1975) 15 Cal.3d 130, Brewer v. Simpson (1960) 53 Cal.2d 567, Lambert v. Commonwealth Land Title Ins. Co. (1991) 53 Cal.3d 1072, and Marketing West, Inc. v. Sanyo Fisher (USA) Corp. (1992) 6 Cal.App.4th 603, none of which was fetched for this sheet. The elements of a Tameny claim are covered by this corpus’s separate wrongful-termination-in-violation-of-public-policy sheet and are not restated here, and this corpus’s at-will presumption sheet covers Guz v. Bechtel National, Inc. (2000) 24 Cal.4th 317 on implied contract. Nothing here states that Acme, Inc. made any promise to Jordan Lee.

WHAT THE CONTINUING VIOLATION DOCTRINE IS, AND THE TWO QUESTIONS IT RAISES
Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. is the California Supreme Court’s treatment of the continuing violation doctrine under the FEHA. The employee there resigned after a five-year period during which she said her employer would not effectively accommodate her disability, and much of the conduct she proved at trial fell outside the filing period. The Court described the doctrine as allowing liability for unlawful employer conduct occurring outside the limitations period when it is sufficiently connected to unlawful conduct within it, and separated two questions that arise when a claim rests partly on older conduct: an evidentiary question, whether the older acts come in as relevant background, and a remedial question, whether the employer is liable for them. Richards decided the second. Before reaching it the Court surveyed the federal case law and noted a treatise’s description of the area as a muddled one, identifying four different federal approaches. The conduct Jordan Lee describes as beginning November 14, 2022 is not characterized here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "That doctrine, described at greater length below, allows liability for unlawful employer conduct occurring outside the statute of limitations if it is sufficiently connected to unlawful conduct within the limitations period."
  — Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. (2001) 26 Cal.4th 798, 26 Cal.4th 798, 802 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2633435/richards-v-ch2m-hill-inc/)
  "Essentially, the continuing violation doctrine comes into play when an employee raises a claim based on conduct that occurred in part outside the limitations period. In such cases, two questions are potentially raised. The first question is evidentiary: Are the alleged acts outside the limitations period admissible as relevant background evidence?"
  — Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. (2001) 26 Cal.4th 798, 26 Cal.4th 798, 812 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2633435/richards-v-ch2m-hill-inc/)
  "The second and more difficult question is remedial: Is an employer liable for actions that take place outside the limitations period if these actions are sufficiently linked to unlawful conduct within the limitations period? It is this second question that is at issue in this case."
  — Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. (2001) 26 Cal.4th 798, 26 Cal.4th 798, 812 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2633435/richards-v-ch2m-hill-inc/)
  "This is so because the doctrine refers not to a single theory, but to a number of different approaches, in different contexts and using a variety of formulations, to extending the statute of limitations in employment discrimination cases."
  — Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. (2001) 26 Cal.4th 798, 26 Cal.4th 798, 813 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2633435/richards-v-ch2m-hill-inc/)
  Known gap: The four federal approaches Richards catalogued — a continuing corporate policy, equitable tolling, the three-factor Berry v. Board of Sup’rs of L.S.U. (5th Cir. 1983) 715 F.2d 971 test, and the Ninth Circuit’s broader course-of-conduct test — are summarized here only as Richards summarizes them; none of those federal decisions, nor Accardi v. Superior Court (1993) 17 Cal.App.4th 341, was fetched for this sheet. The distinction Richards drew between the evidentiary and the remedial question means that an act being outside the filing period does not by itself decide whether evidence of it is admissible; the evidentiary question is governed by the rules of evidence and is not addressed here. Brown, J., filed a dissenting opinion in Richards, which is not quoted in this sheet; the retrieved copy records that George, C. J., Kennard, J., and Chin, J., concurred in the majority opinion and does not record which justices joined the dissent. Nothing here states that any conduct involving Acme, Inc. occurred or was unlawful.

THE THREE-PART TEST AND WHAT “PERMANENCE” MEANS
Richards adopted a modified version of the three-factor test drawn from Berry v. Board of Sup’rs of L.S.U., under which an employer’s persistent failure to reasonably accommodate a disability, or to eliminate a hostile work environment targeting a disabled employee, is a continuing violation if the employer’s unlawful actions are sufficiently similar in kind, have occurred with reasonable frequency, and have not acquired a degree of permanence. On the first factor the Court noted that similar kinds of conduct may take a number of different forms. The modification is in the third factor: rather than the general notice-of-injury idea Berry used, Richards held that permanence in this setting means the employer’s statements and actions make clear to a reasonable employee that further efforts at informal conciliation will be futile. The Court applied the doctrine to the plaintiff’s disability discrimination claim as well as to her harassment claim. Yanowitz v. L’Oreal USA, Inc. later restated the same three factors and the same definition of permanence. Whether anything described about Acme, Inc. would satisfy any of these factors is not determined here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "The first is subject matter. Do the alleged acts involve the same type of discrimination, tending to connect them in a continuing violation? The second is frequency. Are the alleged acts recurring (e.g., a biweekly paycheck) or more in the nature of an isolated work assignment or employment decision? The third factor, perhaps of most importance, is degree of permanence."
  — Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. (2001) 26 Cal.4th 798, 26 Cal.4th 798, 814 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2633435/richards-v-ch2m-hill-inc/)
  "Accordingly, we adopt a modified version of the Berry test. As in Berry, we hold that an employer’s persistent failure to reasonably accommodate a disability, or to eliminate a hostile work environment targeting a disabled employee, is a continuing violation if the employer’s unlawful actions are (1) sufficiently similar in kind—recognizing, as this case illustrates, that similar kinds of unlawful employer conduct, such as acts of harassment or failures to reasonably accommodate disability, may take a number of different forms"
  — Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. (2001) 26 Cal.4th 798, 26 Cal.4th 798, 823 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2633435/richards-v-ch2m-hill-inc/)
  "But consistent with our case law and with the statutory objectives of the FEHA, we further hold that “permanence” in the context of an ongoing process of accommodation of disability, or ongoing disability harassment, should properly be understood to mean the following: that an employer’s statements and actions make clear to a reasonable employee that any further efforts at informal conciliation to obtain reasonable accommodation or end harassment will be futile."
  — Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. (2001) 26 Cal.4th 798, 26 Cal.4th 798, 823 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2633435/richards-v-ch2m-hill-inc/)
  "the employer’s ... actions [were] (1) sufficiently similar in kind—recognizing, as this case illustrates, that similar kinds of unlawful employer conduct, such as acts of harassment or failures to reasonably accommodate disability, may take a number of different forms [citation]; (2) have occurred with reasonable frequency; (3) and have not acquired a degree of permanence."
  — Yanowitz v. L'Oreal USA, Inc. (2005) 36 Cal.4th 1028, 36 Cal.4th 1028, 1059 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2567202/yanowitz-v-loreal-usa-inc/)
  "We also noted that “permanence” properly should be understood to mean “that an employer’s statements and actions make clear to a reasonable employee that any further efforts at informal conciliation to obtain reasonable accommodation or end harassment will be futile.”"
  — Yanowitz v. L'Oreal USA, Inc. (2005) 36 Cal.4th 1028, 36 Cal.4th 1028, 1059, fn. 19 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2567202/yanowitz-v-loreal-usa-inc/)
  "Indeed, in Richards, we expressly applied the continuing violation doctrine to the plaintiff’s disability discrimination claim, as well as to her disability harassment claim."
  — Yanowitz v. L'Oreal USA, Inc. (2005) 36 Cal.4th 1028, 36 Cal.4th 1028, 1057-1058 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2567202/yanowitz-v-loreal-usa-inc/)
  Known gap: The three factors state a test; they do not state a result, and each is a question about a particular record. Richards itself did not decide whether the test was satisfied on its own facts — it reversed and remanded because neither lower court had applied the right standard and the trial court had never considered permanence. Richards framed its holding in terms of failure to accommodate and disability harassment, which were the claims before it; Yanowitz later extended the doctrine to retaliation, and the rest of that development is described in the separate clauses of this sheet. The Berry factors as quoted here are quoted from Richards’s description of Berry, not from the federal opinion, which was not fetched for this sheet, and Fielder v. UAL Corp. (9th Cir. 2000) 218 F.3d 973 is cited only as Richards cites it. The Yanowitz passages quoted in this clause are that court’s quotation of Richards and appear in the Yanowitz majority opinion and in its footnote 19. Nothing here states what Jordan Lee experienced.

WHEN THE CLOCK STARTS ON A CONTINUING COURSE OF CONDUCT
Richards stated the accrual rule that follows from its test. Where an employer engages in a continuing course of unlawful conduct that does not amount to a constructive discharge, the period begins to run not necessarily when the employee first believes rights may have been violated, but either when the course of conduct ends — by the employer stopping or by the employee resigning — or when the employee is on notice that further efforts to end the conduct will be in vain. The Court described the corollary for employers: an employer can start the clock by making clear in a definitive manner that the requests will not be granted. It also set a limit in the other direction, saying that allowing an employee to delay indefinitely would be contrary to the statute of limitations and potentially prejudicial to the employer, and that once the hope of informal conciliation is unreasonable the justification for delay no longer exists. Yanowitz restated the rule as the period beginning when an alleged adverse employment action acquires some degree of permanence or finality. Whether anything occurring in the separation of Jordan Lee had that character is not determined here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Thus, when an employer engages in a continuing course of unlawful conduct under the FEHA by refusing reasonable accommodation of a disabled employee or engaging in disability harassment, and this course of conduct does not constitute a constructive discharge, the statute of limitations begins to run, not necessarily when the employee first believes that his or her rights may have been violated, but rather, either when the course of conduct is brought to an end, as by the employer’s cessation of such conduct or by the employee’s resignation, or when the employee is on notice that further efforts to end the unlawful conduct will be in vain."
  — Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. (2001) 26 Cal.4th 798, 26 Cal.4th 798, 823-824 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2633435/richards-v-ch2m-hill-inc/)
  "Accordingly, an employer who is confronted with an employee seeking accommodation of disability or relief from disability harassment may assert control over its legal relationship with the employee either by accommodating the employee’s requests, or by making clear to the employee in a definitive manner that it will not be granting any such requests, thereby commencing the running of the statute of limitations."
  — Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. (2001) 26 Cal.4th 798, 26 Cal.4th 798, 823-824 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2633435/richards-v-ch2m-hill-inc/)
  "If the employer has made clear in word and deed that the employee’s attempted further reasonable accommodation is futile, then the employee is on notice that litigation, not informal conciliation, is the only alternative for the vindication of his or her rights. Barring a constructive discharge, it is at that point the statute of limitations for the violation begins to run."
  — Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. (2001) 26 Cal.4th 798, 26 Cal.4th 798, 823 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2633435/richards-v-ch2m-hill-inc/)
  "Thus, we reiterate that in a retaliation case, as in a disability accommodation or harassment case, the FEHA statute of limitations begins to run when an alleged adverse employment action acquires some degree of permanence or finality."
  — Yanowitz v. L'Oreal USA, Inc. (2005) 36 Cal.4th 1028, 36 Cal.4th 1028, 1059 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2567202/yanowitz-v-loreal-usa-inc/)
  Known gap: This accrual rule is stated for a continuing course of conduct. Richards expressly carved out constructive discharge, which it treated under Mullins v. Rockwell Internat. Corp. (1997) 15 Cal.4th 731 as accruing on resignation; Mullins was not independently fetched for this sheet and is reported only as Richards describes it, and this corpus’s constructive discharge sheet covers the elements of that doctrine rather than its accrual date. The rule also does not displace Romano for a completed discharge. Richards decided when a period begins, not how long it is, and not whether any tolling or extension applies; the extensions in Government Code section 12960, subdivision (e)(6) and the tolling in subdivision (f) are not addressed here. The date recorded as August 28, 2026 is used in this sheet only to identify the separation, not as a legal conclusion that any period began on it.

RETALIATION CLAIMS AND THE COLLECTIVE VIEW OF A SERIES OF ACTS
Yanowitz v. L’Oreal USA, Inc. extended the doctrine to retaliation. Two holdings in that decision work together. First, on what counts as an adverse employment action under Government Code section 12940, subdivision (h), the Court held that the action must materially affect the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, while directing that the inquiry take account of the affected employee’s circumstances and the workplace context; minor or trivial actions that would do no more than anger or upset are not actionable, but treatment reasonably likely to impair a reasonable employee’s job performance or prospects for advancement or promotion is. Second, the Court held that retaliatory acts may be considered collectively, rejecting any requirement that an employer’s retaliation arrive as one swift blow rather than a series of subtle injuries. The two holdings meet in the limitations analysis: if the doctrine were unavailable, the period would start with the first act of retaliation even though that act might not be actionable standing alone. The Court concluded that the doctrine applies in retaliation cases where the required showing of a continuing course of conduct is made. Nothing here states that Acme, Inc. retaliated against anyone.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Accordingly, although an adverse employment action must materially affect the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment to be actionable, the determination of whether a particular action or course of conduct rises to the level of actionable conduct should take into account the unique circumstances of the affected employee as well as the workplace context of the claim."
  — Yanowitz v. L'Oreal USA, Inc. (2005) 36 Cal.4th 1028, 36 Cal.4th 1028, 1052 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2567202/yanowitz-v-loreal-usa-inc/)
  "Minor or relatively trivial adverse actions or conduct by employers or fellow employees that, from an objective perspective, are reasonably likely to do no more than anger or upset an employee cannot properly be viewed as materially affecting the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment and are not actionable, but adverse treatment that is reasonably likely to impair a reasonable employee’s job performance or prospects for advancement or promotion falls within the reach of the antidiscrimination provisions of sections 12940(a) and 12940(h)."
  — Yanowitz v. L'Oreal USA, Inc. (2005) 36 Cal.4th 1028, 36 Cal.4th 1028, 1054-1055 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2567202/yanowitz-v-loreal-usa-inc/)
  "Contrary to L’Oreal’s assertion that it is improper to consider collectively the alleged retaliatory acts, there is no requirement that an employer’s retaliatory acts constitute one swift blow, rather than a series of subtle, yet damaging, injuries."
  — Yanowitz v. L'Oreal USA, Inc. (2005) 36 Cal.4th 1028, 36 Cal.4th 1028, 1055 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2567202/yanowitz-v-loreal-usa-inc/)
  "Enforcing a requirement that each act separately constitute an adverse employment action would subvert the purpose and intent of the statute."
  — Yanowitz v. L'Oreal USA, Inc. (2005) 36 Cal.4th 1028, 36 Cal.4th 1028, 1056 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2567202/yanowitz-v-loreal-usa-inc/)
  "If, however, we were to foreclose application of the continuing violation doctrine as a matter of law in retaliation cases, the statute of limitations would start running upon the happening of the first act of retaliation, even if that act would not be actionable standing alone."
  — Yanowitz v. L'Oreal USA, Inc. (2005) 36 Cal.4th 1028, 36 Cal.4th 1028, 1058 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2567202/yanowitz-v-loreal-usa-inc/)
  "We believe the better rule is to allow application of the continuing violation doctrine in retaliation cases if the requisite showing of a continuing course of conduct has been made."
  — Yanowitz v. L'Oreal USA, Inc. (2005) 36 Cal.4th 1028, 36 Cal.4th 1028, 1059 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2567202/yanowitz-v-loreal-usa-inc/)
  Known gap: Yanowitz decided these questions at the summary adjudication stage; on the continuing violation point the Court held only that it could not say the doctrine was inapplicable as a matter of law on that record, which is not a finding that any act was retaliatory or timely. The Court’s interpretation of “otherwise discriminate” in section 12940, subdivision (h), including its rejection of the broader “deterrence” standard adopted below and its reliance on Harris v. Forklift Systems, Inc. (1993) 510 U.S. 17 and on federal title VII decisions, is described here only as Yanowitz describes it; none of those federal authorities was fetched for this sheet. It is prepared in connection with the separation of Jordan Lee from Acme, Inc., where the position held was Project Engineer, the date the employer first communicated that the employment would end is stated as March 2, 2026, the date the employment actually ended is stated as August 28, 2026, and the earliest workplace conduct the employee describes is stated as beginning November 14, 2022. Those dates are as supplied by the person preparing this sheet; nothing here verifies them. This sheet is a description of published statutes and California Supreme Court decisions. It is not a complaint, not a filing with the Civil Rights Department, not a court document, not a calculation of any deadline in any particular matter, and not a determination that any conduct described by anyone was unlawful, that any claim exists, or that any claim is timely or untimely.

The continuing violation doctrine is a rule about a filing deadline, so it only makes sense against that deadline. Government Code section 12960 governs the procedure for complaints of practices made unlawful by the FEHA’s employment provisions. Subdivision (c) allows any person claiming to be aggrieved by an alleged unlawful practice to file a verified written complaint with the Civil Rights Department. Subdivision (e)(5) sets the period for an employment complaint under Article 1 of Chapter 6 (Government Code section 12940 and following) at three years from the date the unlawful practice or refusal to cooperate occurred, and subdivision (b) provides that filing an intake form counts as filing, with the verified complaint relating back to the intake form. The statutory period was one year when the decisions described in the rest of this sheet were written; Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. quoted the one-year version of section 12960 as it then read. Section 12993, subdivision (a) supplies the interpretive instruction the courts applied to that period: the FEHA is to be construed liberally. Whether any complaint concerning Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. was filed, and when, is not addressed here.

expectedJSON.body: Romano v. Rockwell Internat., Inc. answered when the clock starts when an employee is told in advance that the employment will end. The employee there was notified in December 1988 that his employment would end, and it ended on May 31, 1991 — an interval of two and a half years during which he continued to be paid. The employer argued, relying on federal authority, that the period ran from the unequivocal notice. The California Supreme Court held otherwise for the FEHA claim, reasoning from the statutory word “occurred”: because section 12960 runs from the date the unlawful practice occurred, and because a discharge is the termination of employment, the practice has not occurred on the date notice is given. The Court added practical reasons — the date of actual termination is usually undisputed while notice is often oral, conditional, or equivocal, and a notice-based rule would force employees to file while still employed, over a harm that had not happened yet. In the separation of Jordan Lee from Acme, Inc., the notice date and the termination date are stated as March 2, 2026 and August 28, 2026; which legal consequence follows from those particular dates is not determined here.

expectedJSON.body: Richards v. CH2M Hill, Inc. is the California Supreme Court’s treatment of the continuing violation doctrine under the FEHA. The employee there resigned after a five-year period during which she said her employer would not effectively accommodate her disability, and much of the conduct she proved at trial fell outside the filing period. The Court described the doctrine as allowing liability for unlawful employer conduct occurring outside the limitations period when it is sufficiently connected to unlawful conduct within it, and separated two questions that arise when a claim rests partly on older conduct: an evidentiary question, whether the older acts come in as relevant background, and a remedial question, whether the employer is liable for them. Richards decided the second. Before reaching it the Court surveyed the federal case law and noted a treatise’s description of the area as a muddled one, identifying four different federal approaches. The conduct Jordan Lee describes as beginning November 14, 2022 is not characterized here.

The modification is in the third factor: rather than the general notice-of-injury idea Berry used, Richards held that permanence in this setting means the employer’s statements and actions make clear to a reasonable employee that further efforts at informal conciliation will be futile. The Court applied the doctrine to the plaintiff’s disability discrimination claim as well as to her harassment claim. Yanowitz v. L’Oreal USA, Inc. later restated the same three factors and the same definition of permanence. Whether anything described about Acme, Inc. would satisfy any of these factors is not determined here.

expectedJSON.body: Richards stated the accrual rule that follows from its test. The Court described the corollary for employers: an employer can start the clock by making clear in a definitive manner that the requests will not be granted. It also set a limit in the other direction, saying that allowing an employee to delay indefinitely would be contrary to the statute of limitations and potentially prejudicial to the employer, and that once the hope of informal conciliation is unreasonable the justification for delay no longer exists. Yanowitz restated the rule as the period beginning when an alleged adverse employment action acquires some degree of permanence or finality. expectedJSON.gap: Morgan itself was not fetched for this sheet and is described only as Yanowitz describes it; a reader comparing the two bodies of law would need the federal opinion and the federal filing deadlines, which are not covered here. Yanowitz declined to adopt Morgan in the retaliation context on the record before it; it did not hold that every FEHA claim escapes a discrete-act analysis, and later California decisions have continued to apply the Richards factors case by case. The passage declining Morgan’s reasoning appears in footnote 18 of the Yanowitz majority opinion, and the passage on the liberal construction of the FEHA limitations period appears in footnote 17; footnote text carries the same authority as the rest of the opinion but is identified here so a reader can locate it. Nothing here compares the merits of any claim Jordan Lee might have under either body of law.
